title: The Love Guru
full_review:
"The Love Guru" (Paramount/Spyglass) is a flat comedy, only fitfully enlivened by some clever gags, with Mike Myers as Pitka, an American-born guru loosely inspired by Maharishi Mahesh Yogi, spiritual guide to the Beatles in the 1960s.

 

Billed as Myers' first comic character since Austin Powers, Pitka is sometimes endearing but more often a poor relation to the late British comic Peter Sellers' memorable gallery of Indian eccentrics.

Jane Bullard (Jessica Alba), the beauteous owner of the Toronto Maple Leafs hockey team -- scorned by the fans because since her family acquired the team in 1967 they have failed to win the Stanley Cup -- enlists Deepak Chopra-wannabe Pitka to bring about the reconciliation of Darren Roanoke, the team's star player (Romany Malco), and his wife, Prudence (Meagan Good).

She's left Darren for his Los Angeles Kings rival, French-Canadian goalie Jacques "Le Coq" Grande (an unrecognizably hirsute Justin Timberlake in a surprising comic turn).

 

If Pitka can help Darren both win back Prudence and overcome his paralyzing mother issues, the athlete will get back his prowess on the ice and lead the team to victory.

Alba makes a nice level-headed counterpart to Myers' shenanigans, and there are some amusing big-name cameos throughout, while Mahatma Gandhi may be spinning in his grave as his Oscar-winning cinematic interpreter, Ben Kingsley, offers a wacky comic turn as Pitka's cross-eyed spiritual mentor, shown in flashback training the young Pitka and Chopra side by side.

And there is some further funny business involving hokey Bollywood musicals, Mariska Hargitay (whose name is Pitka's trademark mantra), and Oprah Winfrey, to whose guest couch Pitka desperately aspires. But finally, the satirical jibes at celebrity and bogus Indian mysticism wear thin.

Unabashedly vulgar and tasteless, the film, which wallows in endless penis jokes and fairly yucky potty humor, is directed at an often tentative pace by Marco Schnabel.

Much of the humor (script by Myers and Graham Gordy) and gags fails to land. At the preview screening attended, the audience remained silently unresponsive for stretches, with the film feeling too long by half.

The inevitable romance between Pitka and Jane is rather sweet (if improbable), and for reasons not made clear until late in the film, remains platonic There are some moderately redemptive elements such as Pitka working to restore Darren's marriage and ultimately forgoing his lifelong obsession with celebrity to do the "right thing."

But though the overall tone is lightheartedly cartoonish, the sheer volume of coarseness finally pushes this into the morally offensive category. As one preview spectator exclaimed loudly near the end of the screening, "This is baaaaad." (No guru needed for that enlightened judgment!)

The film contains much sexual and scatological humor and innuendo, some crude language, adultery and an implied premarital relationship, drug references and comic violence. The USCCB Office for Film & Broadcasting classification is O -- morally offensive. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is PG-13 -- parents strongly cautioned. Some material may be inappropriate for children under 13.
